steps: Start setting up your GmbH in month 2. It usually takes 6 to 12 weeks in Germany.
Use employer of record for your first hires until month 5, so you can hire straight away.
Move your team onto your own company in month 5, when it becomes cheaper to run than employer of record.
flags: In Germany an employer of record must hold a labour leasing licence, and the same person can usually be placed with you for at most 18 months. Your plan keeps people in the country beyond month 18, so this counts as a risk.
People who work only for you, full-time and under your direction, are usually treated as employees. Using contractors for them is risky, so employer of record or your own company is the safer choice.
Running a company where you do not work in the local language costs more, so the running cost has been raised by 30%.

review.summary: The recommended route is to start with an employer of record and move the team into your own German company (GmbH) in month 5, when running your own company becomes cheaper. The plan costs 77,520 EUR on top of pay over 24 months, against 138,020 EUR for staying with an employer of record, a saving of 60,500 EUR.
review.driver: The financial check favours your own company, because the cost of running it falls below the employer of record fee at month 5, when the team reaches 6 people. The risk and strategic checks also point that way: people who work only for you are usually treated as employees, and your plan keeps staff beyond the 18-month employer of record limit.
risks: German employer of record placements are usually limited to 18 months, and your plan keeps some staff beyond month 18, so those placements would need a different arrangement.
Setup must be ready by month 5, but the setup typically takes 6 to 12 weeks from month 2, so there is little room for delay.
Running the company without German language skills raises running costs by 30%, so the 2,600 EUR monthly running cost assumption depends on that uplift being correct.
